stimulus.text:
Mason Locke Weems, The Life of Washington, first published in 1800, was a best-selling biography of George Washington. In the fifth edition, published in 1806, Weems added the story of young Washington and the cherry tree:

“I can’t tell a lie, Pa; you know I can’t tell a lie. I did cut it with my hatchet.” — “Run to my arms, you dearest boy,” cried his father in transports, “run to my arms; glad am I, George, that you killed my tree; for you have paid me for it a thousand fold. Such an act of heroism in my son is more worth than a thousand trees, though blossomed with silver, and their fruits of purest gold.”

No evidence supports the story as a real event; Weems said he had heard it from a friend of the Washington family.
stimulus.source_note: Mason Locke Weems, The Life of Washington (1800; fifth edition 1806). Public domain.

source: original; stimulus quoted verbatim from Mason Locke Weems, The Life of Washington, fifth edition (1806). Public domain.

primary_sources: Mason Locke Weems, The Life of Washington (1800; fifth edition 1806)

stem: Why did Weems add the cherry-tree story to his biography of Washington?

options.text: To prove that Washington had owned a cherry orchard as a boy.
options.misconception: The story is about honesty, not about proving Washington owned an orchard.

options.text: To hold Washington up as a model of honesty for young Americans.
To show that Washington’s father punished him harshly for lying.
options.misconception: In the story the father praises the boy’s honesty, and he does not punish him.

options.text: To record Washington’s own account of his childhood.
options.misconception: Background: the story came from Weems, not from Washington, and no evidence supports it as a real event.

rationales.B: The boy confesses, his father praises his honesty, and the story teaches young readers to tell the truth.
rationales.A: The story never tries to prove Washington owned an orchard.
rationales.C: The father embraces the boy and praises him; there is no harsh punishment.
rationales.D: Weems wrote the story himself; it is not Washington’s own account.
rationales.general:
1. The story ends with the boy confessing, “I did cut it with my hatchet.”
2. His father praises the confession as worth more than a thousand trees.
3. Background: Weems wrote a best-selling life of Washington for American readers, first published in 1800.
4. So the story holds Washington up as a model of honesty for young Americans.
Remember: a story in a biography can teach a value even when it is not a fact.
